This is not something that I'm worried about, especially since we've seen much bigger liquidation events in the past.

But this time, I'm more concerned about the negative Bitcoin ETF inflows.

1. ETF Outflows

$2.35B left Bitcoin ETFs in just two weeks. That's a reversal of the buying pressure that helped BTC recover earlier this year.

2. Nvidia

Nvidia dropped 13% in the past week, with BTC falling alongside it. It's not true 100% of the time, but crypto often follows big tech's moves.

3. Interest Rates

U.S. inflation is proving stubborn, and traders are betting on another Fed rate hike. As per usual, higher interest rates make assets like BTC less attractive.

4. Strategy

MSCI is removing $MSTR from its indexes. That could trigger forced stock selling and make it harder for @Strategy to raise money for more BTC purchases.

5. Liquidations

Around $1.5B was liquidated in 24 hours, compared to $19B during the Oct 2025 crash.

I don't think liquidations alone explain this selloff. We can call bottom once ETF inflows return and BTC reclaims its 200-day moving average.

Until then, be smart and protect your capital.

I ran the numbers on BlackRock's Bitcoin ETF, and the average buyer got in around $81K.

BTC is at $65K, so they're sitting on about a 19% loss.

Yet...almost none of them have sold yet. Here's why that matters for you:

The short version: don't count on a fast recovery, don't chase bounces, and DCA monthly until the signals at the end flip.

/1 The ETF crowd hasn't sold yet

I took every day of flows into BlackRock's ETF (IBIT, by far the biggest) since launch and weighted it by that day's BTC price. 

Net inflows come out to about $80.7K'ish per BTC. 

BTC has spent most of 2026 below that line. In Sep–Oct it finally got above it, ran to about $86K, and held for a month. Then the Binance hack hit, and it fell 20%.

Since the hack, about $3B has left the spot BTC ETFs, $2.35B of it from IBIT, with outflows on 10 of the last 11 trading days.

But IBIT still holds about 795K BTC, only 4% below its peak. Most ETF holders haven't sold, instead they're sitting on a loss and waiting.

What to do: That's a lot of people who'll be tempted to sell when they get back to even. If you bought higher, don't count on a quick trip back to $81K to get out. 

If you trade, a bounce toward $81K is a place to take some profit, not to add. I'd only buy more aggressively once BTC is back above $81K and ETF flows have turned positive.

/2 Crypto's cash is shrinking

Stablecoin supply shrank by $15.5B in the last 30 days. Three quarters of that was USDT and USDC, the main dollars people use to buy crypto.

Less cash on the sidelines means fewer buyers for the dip.

The long-term picture is different. Stablecoin payments hit $482B in the first 9 months of this year, up 45% (per Allium). People are using crypto dollars more, even while they hold fewer of them.

What to do: Don't chase green days. Stick to your DCA. And watch USDT & USDC supply (free on DefiLlama). 

When it starts growing again, the buyers are coming back.

/3 Buybacks are a cushion, not a floor

At its current pace, pump is buying back about 18% of its circulating market cap a year. It's still down 35% since the hack.

Hyperliquid buys back about 5% a year, and HYPE is down 17%. That's better than BTC (-20%), ETH (-23%) & SOL (-29%).

The difference is the business behind it. Hyperliquid's buybacks over the last 30 days ran above its 12-month average. Pump ran below.

What to do: Before you buy a token for its buybacks, pull up its revenue. If the last few months are trending down, skip it, no matter how big the buyback looks.

/4 So what am I doing?

DCA monthly. At these prices, I'm happy to keep buying BTC and HYPE every month. DCA keeps it simpler than trying to time this.

Keep cash. If the selling isn't done, you'll want ammo lower.

No leverage. Not in this market, and it's not something I usually do anyway.

Be VERY Picky on alts. If I buy alts, only ones with a growing business behind the buybacks.

/5 What would tell me it's turned

USDT & USDC growing again.

ETF flows turning positive.

The Fed done hiking, and then cutting.

BTC back above $81K and holding it.

What are you doing in this market?

Anthony, the "spy" story appears to be as fake as Russiagate. Here are the facts as I understand them.

(1) First, Alice Huang was at a company called Megaspeed[1], which everyone agrees bought Nvidia chips to sell to Southeast Asian companies called neoclouds. This is in itself completely legal under US law.

(2) However, some both inside and outside the admin didn't like this. They want to block Chinese nationals from accessing cloud services with Nvidia GPUs even if those servers are located outside China. Fine, but the so-called Remote Access Security Act (RASA) to block this has passed the House but not the Senate, and is not law[2].

(3) Singapore's government also looked into this when Alice Huang was on their soil[3] and didn't find any evidence that Megaspeed was actually selling chips to China illegally — let alone that she was a "Chinese spy." They did give her an entry ban, but that's like a visa denial.

(4) The related point is that it's not actually illegal to sell Nvidia chips to China! Since the Biden admin, there has been a complex and constantly-shifting set of export restrictions on chips. As of right now, Nvidia is allowed to sell H200s[4] to China, and indeed has designed these to comply with applicable law.

(5) But you know what...China actually also doesn't want Nvidia chips in China [5,6], because they want to build up their homegrown chip industry. The Nvidia chips are so good that China doesn't want to remain dependent on American chips, or vulnerable to possible US backdoors.

(6) The broader point is that this is an argument between nationalists and capitalists. Nationalists argue that US companies shouldn't even get close to selling to China, and shouldn't even be selling to neoclouds, even if it's "technically" legal. Capitalists argue that it's impossible for American companies to dominate world markets without, you know, being allowed to dominate world markets by actually competing in them. And that it's one thing to restrict physical sales to China, and quite another to require proof-of-citizenship for every single cloud access.

(7) Here's the thing: it doesn't make sense for one of the (few!) industries where America has a trade surplus with China to be summarily cut off, if you're worried about trade surpluses. It doesn't make sense to remove your number one AI CEO, if you want to be number one in AI. And it truly doesn't make sense to do to Jensen Huang what the communists did to Jack Ma[7], if your goal is fighting communism.

(8) So, to summarize: there's no proof of spying, as Blanche at DOJ has admitted[8], which rebuts your FBI/DOJ points. The Wachtell investigation you raise is just an in-house thing[9] ordered by the Nvidia board. And so all that's left is some affairs, which society has agreed is not disqualifying, given the realities of both Clinton and Trump.

In short: do you want a communist society like China, where Jack Ma's company can be stolen from him overnight on false pretenses? Or do you want some semblance of rule of law? If so, you should support the restoration of Jensen Huang to the company he built.

Citations follow in the next tweet.

I’m realizing that some SaaS businesses could make tens of millions in additional revenue by building RL environments for AI labs.

Take a KYB startup. You’ve spent years collecting company records across 150 countries, cleaning them, linking entities, and building APIs on top. 

You have millions of real-world investigations hiding in your database. You can turn them into tasks for AI agents:

“Find the CEO of this company and cite the official document.”

“Identify everyone who indirectly owns more than 25% of this business. Follow the ownership chain across France, Luxembourg, and Singapore.”

“Compare this company’s onboarding application with the registry filings. What’s missing or inconsistent?”

Give the agent tools to search the records and read the documents. Then use your structured data to check the answer: did it find the right entities, calculate the ownership correctly, and cite the right evidence?

Now you have an environment where agents can practice millions of investigations and get a reward when they get them right.

These aren’t just KYB tasks because the same skills matter for due diligence, investing, procurement, compliance, and a ton of other knowledge work.

If you can show that training on your environment makes models better at these tasks, I think you’ll find a buyer for a lot of $$$

The more I hang out with top AI researchers, the more I realize how many of them are exploring architectures beyond the standard Transformer.

JEPA, diffusion models, Mamba, state-space models, etc. So many radically different approaches being explored in parallel.

It seems almost inconceivable that we won’t see a major architectural breakthrough.

And by breakthrough, I mean something that delivers better frontier intelligence with significantly less training compute.

That doesn’t mean we’ll use less compute overall. Quite the opposite, total compute consumption will keep growing. But we’ll get much better performance for every unit of compute spent.
